<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is a static website to showcase Nerfies – the project behind “Deformable Neural Radiance Fields.” The website (at https://nerfies.github.io) is built entirely with front-end assets, meaning that its architecture is centered around static resources (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, videos, etc.) without a dedicated backend service.

Below is a detailed guide tailored to this project’s purpose and structure, explaining how to draw an accurate system design diagram:

1. Project Type & Purpose
   - Type: A static, front-end website.
   - Purpose: To present information and multimedia about the Nerfies project and research. It functions as a showcase with supporting media (CSS for styling, JS for interactive behavior, and various videos/images to demonstrate the project’s functionalities).

2. Analyzing the File Structure
   - Top-Level Files & Directories:
     • index.html – This is the main HTML file that defines the page layout.
     • static/ – Contains several subdirectories:
       • css/ – Holds style files (e.g., “index.css” and a Bulma mapping file) that affect the look and feel.
       • js/ – Contains JavaScript files (such as “bulma-carousel.js”, “bulma-slider.js”, “index.js”) responsible for interactive behavior.
       • images/ – Holds image assets to be used on the site.
       • videos/ – Contains multiple video files that are likely used for demonstrations.
       • interpolation/ – Appears to include additional resources, possibly related to visual interpolation or demonstrative stacking effects.
   - Architectural Implications:
     • The site has a single-page entry point with supporting assets grouped by type.
     • The division into specific directories suggests clear separation of concerns (e.g., presentation with CSS, interactivity with JS, multimedia content separately).

3. Insights from the README
   - The README confirms that this repository is solely for the Nerfies website.
   - It includes attribution information for users who might want to cite the research paper linked to the project.
   - Although it does not provide an internal architecture diagram itself, the content reinforces that the website’s sole responsibility is display and media delivery.

4. Creating the System Design Diagram
   a. Main Components:
      - End User (Browser): Initiates a request to load the website.
      - Web Server/Hosting (e.g., GitHub Pages): Delivers the index.html and static assets.
      - Core HTML File (index.html): Acts as the entry point for the website.
      - CSS Assets (static/css): Style definitions that control layout and presentation.
      - JavaScript Assets (static/js): Scripts that enable interactivity (including libraries for carousels or sliders).
      - Multimedia Assets (static/images, static/videos, static/interpolation): Images, videos, and additional visual resources used to demonstrate aspects of the Nerfies project.
      
   b. Relationships and Interactions:
      - The Browser requests index.html, which then references and loads CSS, JS, and multimedia assets.
      - JavaScript code (e.g., for carousels or sliders) might interact with media assets dynamically.
      - Static assets and media are served by the hosting provider (in this case likely GitHub Pages).
      
   c. Key Architectural Patterns:
      - Separation of concerns: Layout (HTML), styling (CSS), and behavior (JS) are maintained in separate directories.
      - Static content delivery: The absence of a backend means that the diagram should focus on front-end dependency flows.
      
   d. Relevant Technologies & Frameworks:
      - Bulma CSS: Indicated by files like “bulma-carousel.js”, “bulma-slider.js” and CSS map files.
      - Plain HTML, JavaScript, and CSS are used throughout.
      
5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to This Project Type
   - Since this is a static website, emphasize the division between the client’s browser and the set of static files.
   - Show how the index.html bootstraps the application by referencing external style sheets and scripts.
   - Highlight that there is no backend logic – all interactivity is handled client-side with JavaScript.
   - Demonstrate component grouping (e.g., multimedia assets being split between images, videos, and interpolation resources).

6. Instructing on Diagram Details
   - Use clear labels for each component:
     • Label a box "Browser" to depict the user’s point of interaction.
     • Label a box "GitHub Pages (or Host)" for the static web server.
     • Detail a component labeled "index.html" connected to:
         - "CSS" (with subcomponents such as Bulma and custom styling),
         - "JavaScript" (including carousel and slider functionality),
         - "Multimedia Assets" (several subcategories: Images, Videos, Interpolation).
   - Include directional arrows:
     • An arrow from "Browser" to "GitHub Pages (Host)" showing the site request.
     • Arrows from "index.html" to its dependent resources (CSS, JS, multimedia).
   - Use color coding or shapes:
     • Different shapes/colors for presentation (HTML), styling (CSS), behavior (JS), and media (Images/Videos).
     • Consider using a solid box for static files and a dashed box for external services or libraries as needed.
     
7. Emphasize Detailed Capturing of Essential Elements
   - Ensure each key resource is represented.
   - Avoid oversimplification: include all major static directories in the diagram.
   - Clearly indicate the flow: “Browser → index.html → static assets (CSS, JS, multimedia)”.
   - Use annotations to briefly explain the role of each component (e.g., “JS: Handles interactive carousels and UI effects”).
   
By following these guidelines, you can create an accurate and detailed system design diagram that represents the website’s architecture. This diagram will effectively communicate the separation of concerns (HTML, CSS, JS, and multimedia), the relationships between content and assets, and the overall static nature of the project.
</explanation>
